SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images

Rundong Luo   \par Yunong Liu   \par Di Cao   \par
Matthew Tancik   \par Shyamal Buch   \par Colton Stearns   \par Wenqi Xian Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.

1 Introduction

Evaluating the quality and robustness of action policies remains a fundamental bottleneck in robotics. While physical execution is the gold standard, on-robot evaluations are notoriously difficult to scale: they demand expensive hardware, human supervision, and repeated trials across tasks and conditions [li2024simpler]. Consequently, simulation is a powerful alternative that enables large-scale policy evaluation [yang2026robolab]. However, scaling these environments remains difficult, as constructing realistic scenes requires substantial manual effort [jain2025polaris].

Recent advances in agentic reconstruction and 3D generation have made real-to-sim scene reconstruction a promising route to scaling simulation environments [viga2026, chen2026sam3d, simfoundry2026]. In fact, real-to-sim digital twins go beyond mere scaling: they capture the objects and arrangements of physical workspaces and let anyone turn a single photo into a simulation environment for policy evaluation. Yet, despite recent progress in real-to-sim, balancing high-quality 3D reconstruction with faithful, robot-ready simulation physics remains challenging [ma2026rest3d, chen2026agentic]. Even when a reconstruction is physically settled, objects can move away from their observed positions, producing a stable scene that no longer matches the robot’s workspace. To bridge this gap, we propose SceneRig, an agentic system for simulation-ready 3D scene reconstruction from a single image. SceneRig addresses this problem by coupling image-guided pose refinement with physical validation for faithful trajectory replay and policy evaluation.

Making this coupling effective requires the agent to inspect the effects of physical simulation and use that feedback to guide further corrections. Even GPT-6 Astra struggles to achieve accurate, physically stable object placement through VIGA or a general-purpose coding agent when the reconstructed scenes are evaluated after physical settling (Table 4). SceneRig’s core contribution is therefore a harness that connects the agent’s visual reasoning with geometric and physical tools for accurate, stable scene reconstruction. The agent uses the updated scene and feedback from the edit to decide what to investigate or correct next.

More concretely, SceneRig uses a flexible, modular harness with four stages. First, SceneRig builds a relational scene graph, identifying objects and their support relationships. Next, scene object creation uses 2D and 3D vision models to estimate metric geometry and reconstruct object meshes. We then assign physical properties and initialize object placement through geometric alignment and support-ordered settling. Third, specialized agents construct the surrounding geometry, materials, and lighting, with strict rule-based verification gates for geometry and visual verification of all three. Finally, and most importantly, SceneRig executes a physical edit-and-validate loop. The agent selects which object to adjust and whether to change its position, scale, or orientation; geometric and physical tools search for an adjustment and test its effects in simulation. Although the current implementation leverages specific state-of-the-art models, SceneRig is designed to incorporate future foundation models.

We evaluate SceneRig on diverse images, spanning synthetic renderings, real robot workspaces, AI-generated images, and in-the-wild smartphone captures. We demonstrate that SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D object placement over existing methods, with all evaluated scenes passing physical stability checks (Tables 1, 2). Beyond geometric reconstruction, we show that SceneRig yields robot-ready environments (Figure 1), supporting both real-to-sim policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay. In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce SceneRig, an agentic system that reconstructs simulation-ready digital twins from a single image, prioritizing physical grounding in addition to visual similarity.

  • •

    We build a modular harness that equips agents with geometric and physical tools. Through iterative edit-and-validate loops, SceneRig directly incorporates physics into pose refinement.

  • •

    SceneRig improves reconstruction quality and robotics performance over single-image real-to-sim systems. Compared with the baseline, it increases open-loop trajectory replay success from 36% to 80% and episode-level agreement with real-world policy result from 54% to 69%.

2 Related Work

Single-Image Scene Reconstruction. Object-centric reconstruction recovers individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Supervised methods predict geometry or retrieve assets: Total3D [nie2020total3d] predicts indoor layout and meshes, while ROCA [gumerli2022roca] retrieves and aligns CAD models. Without object annotations, uORF [yu2022uorf] and uOCF [luo2024uocf] learn compositional neural fields from multi-view images to separate objects and backgrounds. For explicit meshes, generative methods reconstruct instances separately and align them [dogaru2025gen3dsr, zhou2024dpa, han2025reparo, zhao2025depr], while MIDI [huang2025midi] jointly generates multiple objects. CAST [yao2025cast] combines occlusion-completed object generation with pose refinement using scene relations and signed-distance constraints. SAM3D [chen2026sam3d] predicts object geometry, texture, and camera-relative layout. However, visual fidelity alone does not ensure physical stability or readiness for simulation.

Agentic 3D Scene Creation. VLM agents construct 3D scenes through tool use and iterative feedback [hu2024scenecraft, huang2024blenderalchemy]. To ground generation and editing in scene structure, liu2025agentic3d maintain labeled point clouds and scene relations. SceneWeaver [yang2025sceneweaver] adaptively selects synthesis and editing tools, while Scenethesis [ling2025scenethesis] combines language-based planning with generated-image guidance and geometric constraints. Beyond planning and tool selection, SAGE [xia2026sage] and SceneSmith [pfaff2026scenesmith] use editor-critic loops for indoor scene generation. For precise placement, agents also use numerical solvers [yang2024holodeck, sun2025layoutvlm, wang2026physcensis].

Agentic workflows also support reconstruction from visual references. VIGA [viga2026] reconstructs 3D scenes with a generator–verifier loop, while SEIG [seig2026] extends this approach to refine geometry, materials, and lighting sequentially. SceneConductor [kim2026sceneconductor] initializes layouts, builds environments from point maps, and delegates local corrections to specialist agents. For evaluation, BlenderGym [gu2025blendergym] benchmarks graphics editing, while IR3D-Bench [liu2025ir3dbench] evaluates scene understanding through agentic inverse rendering. In contrast, SceneRig’s agent corrects objects using geometry- and physics-grounded tools.

Physically Grounded Real-to-Sim. Real-to-sim aims at building interactive environments for robot learning and evaluation. RialTo [torne2024rialto], Re3Sim [han2025re3sim], and HoloScene [xia2025holoscene] recover interactive assets from video or scans. Agentic Real2Sim [chen2026agentic] turns a recorded robot–object interaction into a simulatable twin. Our closest baseline, SimFoundry [simfoundry2026], reconstructs editable digital twins from video and generates digital cousins for real-to-sim policy evaluation and sim-to-real policy training. For data generation without dynamics simulation, Real2Render2Real [yu2025real2render2real] renders robot training images from scans.

Concurrent single-image methods use several correction strategies. TableVerse [tableverse2026] resolves collisions through geometric translations before settling; ϕ\phi-Scene [li2026phiscene] optimizes clearance and settles objects in support order. REST3D [ma2026rest3d] optimizes poses with cross-entropy optimization, while RoboSnap [zhang2026robosnap] alternates signed-distance optimization with settling. SimuScene [lee2026simuscene] uses simulated displacement to trigger shape stretching or regeneration. In SceneRig, an agent identifies misplaced objects and calls geometry- and physics-grounded tools to correct them. These tools search for pose adjustments and test edits in simulation, returning feedback to guide further inspection and correction.

Simulation for Policy Evaluation. kadian2020sim2real tune simulation to improve sim–real correlation. SIMPLER [li2024simpler] calibrates controllers from trajectories and matches backgrounds and textures. PolaRiS [jain2025polaris] combines Gaussian splatting with policy co-training on real and simulated data; REALM [sedlacek2026realm] calibrates robot dynamics through replay and tests visual, semantic, and behavioral generalization. Following these, we assess our system through real-sim policy rollout agreement, task success-rate correlation, and open-loop trajectory replay.

3 Method

Given a single RGB image, we reconstruct an editable, simulation-ready 3D scene that matches its appearance and object arrangement. The system primarily targets tabletop scenes for robotics and can also process room scenes by treating the floor as the main support surface.

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote movable objects and ℛ\mathcal{R} denote root surfaces, such as tables, floors, and walls. Each entity has a persistent identity and a state defined by

xv=(Mv,τv,θvphys,Xv),v∈V=𝒪∪ℛ.x_{v}=\left(M_{v},\tau_{v},\theta_{v}^{\mathrm{phys}},X_{v}\right),\qquad v\in V=\mathcal{O}\cup\mathcal{R}. (1)

Here, MvM_{v} is geometry, τv\tau_{v} appearance, θvphys\theta_{v}^{\mathrm{phys}} collision and physical properties, and XvX_{v} a metric transform with translation, rotation, and scale. Illumination is LL, and the scene graph is

G=(V,E),E=Esup∪Esurf,G=(V,E),\qquad E=E_{\mathrm{sup}}\cup E_{\mathrm{surf}}, (2)

where EsupE_{\mathrm{sup}} links objects to direct supports and EsurfE_{\mathrm{surf}} records structural relations among roots.

Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline. We describe relational scene graph construction and scene object creation under Section 3.1, followed by Agentic scene construction (Section 3.2) and physics-grounded object pose refinement (Section 3.3).

3.1 Relational and Metric Initialization

We first recover which entities are present, how they support one another, and where they lie in metric 3D. This relational and geometric evidence guides object reconstruction and physical settling.

Relational parsing. A VLM proposes movable objects 𝒪\mathcal{O}, root surfaces ℛ\mathcal{R}, and their support and structural relations, with a distinct description for each instance. MolmoPoint [molmopoint] localizes each entity from its description, and its predicted points select instance masks from SAM3 [sam3] candidates for that category. Subsequent checks recover objects omitted from the initial inventory, repair split or merged masks, and revise root surfaces and their relations. For occluded objects, we optionally remove foreground occluders with LanPaint [zheng2025lanpaint] and re-segment the target. Entity identities persist throughout reconstruction (Appendix ).

Metric initialization. The scene graph tells us what is present and how entities are related, but not their metric placement in 3D. We use MoGe-2 [wang2025moge2] to estimate camera intrinsics and a dense metric 3D point map. When metric depth and calibrated intrinsics are available, such as from a robot’s RGB-D camera, they replace these estimates. A plane fitted to the main support defines a gravity-aligned coordinate frame in which the support lies at z=0z=0. Fitted planes and estimated contact geometry also provide geometric evidence for validating the proposed scene relations. SAM3D [chen2026sam3d] reconstructs each movable object’s mesh and appearance from the image and its instance mask. We initialize its transform by translating and uniformly scaling the mesh to align with the corresponding metric 3D points. Finally, we estimate the physical properties for simulation following SceneSmith [pfaff2026scenesmith].

Support-ordered physical settling. With the support graph and metric object estimates in place, we settle the reconstructed objects while preserving their observed arrangement. Settling the full scene at once can cause objects to drift, topple, or resolve collisions in ways that differ from the image evidence. Thus, we settle objects in parent-before-child order under GG. Each object is placed against its support and previously settled objects and simulated with PhysX in Isaac Sim. We then use ICP (adjusting translation, scale, and yaw) to improve alignment with its masked 3D observations and simulate it again. Guarded fallbacks may adjust collision geometry and physical properties to obtain a resting configuration; Appendix details these adjustments and the validation procedure.

3.2 Agentic Scene Construction

With objects settled, we reconstruct root geometry (Mr,Xr)(M_{r},X_{r}), materials τr\tau_{r}, and lighting LL in separate stages sharing a persistent Blender scene. Following SEIG [seig2026], each stage edits one variable group. It pairs an editing agent with an independent verifier, both of which receive the scene graph, the current scene snapshot, and the permitted edits. The editor modifies scene code and renders the result, and the verifier compares the render with the reference image, then approves it or requests corrections within the same scope. Each revision continues from the updated scene, preserving earlier work across iterations and stages.

Scene structure. The geometry agent constructs root surfaces in ℛ\mathcal{R} as static colliders, positioning and orienting them with RANSAC-fitted planes and inferring their shapes and sizes from the input image; they must satisfy the required relations in EsurfE_{\mathrm{surf}}. Imported object geometry and appearance remain fixed; objects move only to correct measured contact defects or clear position mismatches.

VLM agents can produce visually plausible geometry that violates support or contact constraints, such as tables intersecting walls or objects floating above surfaces. Whereas VIGA and SEIG leave all checking to the verifier, we add a deterministic check_rules gate that the editing agent must pass before verifier review. The gate checks root placement, object support, and interpenetration, and reports the first failing level with the affected entities. It enforces a minimum geometric standard, leaving the verifier to assess visual alignment, including object placement and background geometry.

Material and lighting. Once the structure is fixed, the material agent updates only root-surface materials and textures, including color, roughness, and surface patterns. The lighting agent then adjusts illumination and exposure to match the shadows, color, and contrast of the input image. Both stages leave background geometry, object placement, and object appearance unchanged, so pose refinement operates on fixed background geometry and rendering conditions.

3.3 Physics-Grounded Object Pose Refinement

After reconstructing the surrounding scene, we refine the object transforms XoX_{o} to correct placement errors that remain after initialization. A naive approach asks the VLM agent to adjust coordinates directly, e.g., by translating an object 0.050.05 units in scene code. However, lacking intrinsic metric grounding, agents often hallucinate these magnitudes, causing collisions or instability. We therefore use an investigation and editing loop in which the agent diagnoses placement errors and calls tools to search for corrections and test them in simulation.

Investigate–edit loop. A single agent session runs this loop in the persistent scene. Every object in 𝒪\mathcal{O} must be investigated at least once, and the agent may revisit objects as their surroundings change. The Investigate tool returns paired crops from the input image and current render, geometric measurements, and support information. Using this information, the agent decides which object to adjust and whether to change its position, scale, or orientation. For example, if an object looks too small in the render, the agent checks whether to move it closer to the camera or enlarge its mesh.

The agent passes the selected object and edit type to the Move tool, which supports horizontal translation, uniform scaling, and yaw adjustment. The tool determines the adjustment magnitude through bounded coarse-to-fine search, using the original pose as a baseline. Translation and scale scores combine silhouette overlap with depth; yaw combines centered silhouette overlap with DINOv2 features [oquab2024dinov2] from object crops. Appendix formalizes these scores in Eq. ().

Physical validation. For routine bounded moves, the Move tool then simulates the selected candidate only if it improves alignment. Physical checks reject capsize or excessive drift, and substantial new or worsened penetration. An update is retained only if these checks pass and its post-settling acceptance score matches or exceeds the baseline (Eq. ()); otherwise, the previous state is restored. If a support moves or is resized, its dependents in EsupE_{\mathrm{sup}} are repositioned and resettled as needed.

When bounded moves are insufficient, the agent can specify pose changes directly through the scene-code editing tool Edit. The tool settles affected objects in support order and returns the simulated render and physical diagnostics. The agent then decides whether to retain or undo the result. Appendix details search objectives and special cases.

Context management and prompt caching. We summarize older interaction rounds in blocks, retaining a log of actions, scores, and outcomes and replacing outdated images with references to saved artifacts. We retain the target image, stage-entry snapshot, and recent evidence. A per-object state table sits after the cache breakpoint, so measurements, pending checks, and budgets can change without invalidating the reusable prompt prefix. In our evaluation benchmark (Sec. 4), 84.1% of pose-refinement input tokens are served from cache (Appendix ; Figure ).

Scene delivery and USD export. After refinement, a joint gravity simulation sets the final object transforms. We bake procedural materials and export meshes, textures, lights, and camera state to USD, preserving object identities, collision geometry, and physical properties for simulation. Appendix details conversion and simulator-side validation.

4 Experiments

We evaluate SceneRig’s reconstruction fidelity, object recovery, 3D layout, and physical stability (Sec. 4.2). We then examine physics-grounded placement and the effects of the VLM backbone and reconstruction harness (Sec. 4.3). Section 5 evaluates robotics applications; Appendix provides additional analyses and results.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Baselines. We compare with four baselines: VIGA [viga2026], REST3D [ma2026rest3d], SceneConductor [kim2026sceneconductor], and SimFoundry [simfoundry2026]. To support object-centric evaluation and simulation, we augment VIGA’s system prompt with a simple object-grouping contract: all parts of each movable object share a single empty Blender parent. We also evaluate SAM3D∗, which shares SceneRig’s segmentation, camera, objects, and scene context but retains SAM3D’s predicted poses without our metric grounding, physical settling, or pose refinement. We use Claude Opus 5 as the default VLM wherever applicable. With GPT-6 Astra, we also compare against Codex, a general-purpose harness that reconstructs the scene directly in Blender without external models. Appendices and provide implementation details and full harness results.

Data. Our benchmark contains 80 tabletop images, including 44 simulator renderings from RoboDojo [chen2026robodojo] and RoboLab [yang2026robolab] with ground-truth object identities and 3D positions. The remainder comprise real robot workspace images, Internet or AI-generated images, and smartphone photos. We evaluate source-view fidelity, perceptual preference, and physical stability on all scenes, and object-centric reconstruction and 3D layout on the simulator subset.

Metrics. We report full-frame PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and nCLIP. Object-centric PSNR∗/SSIM∗ use object regions only (exclude background and table), while LPIPS∗/nCLIP∗ average the per-object crop scores. Instance metrics are adjusted Rand index (ARI), foreground IoU, and object-count MAE. For 3D layout, optimal subpattern assignment (OSPA) [schuhmacher2008ospa] at 5/10 cm cutoffs penalizes position errors and unmatched objects; F1@10 uses one-to-one 3D matches within 10 cm. To account for differences in scale conventions across methods, we align each reconstructed layout to ground truth using a single global scale factor before computing OSPA and F1. GPT-5.6-terra and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B compare reconstruction pairs for completeness, layout, and appearance using the input image and both candidates’ source- and nearby-view renders. We summarize preferences with mean-centered Bradley–Terry scores (inter-judge Cohen’s κ=0.87\kappa=0.87). An object passes the stability test if its displacement after 5 s is below 50 mm and its final velocity is zero; a scene passes only if every object passes. Check details in Appendices and .

4.2 Reconstruction Quality

Reconstruction fidelity and stability. SceneRig achieves the best source-view PSNR, LPIPS, and nCLIP and the highest VLM preference scores across all three criteria (Table 1). VIGA and SceneConductor often fail the stability test, while REST3D’s higher SSIM does not translate into accurate object recovery or placement. SimFoundry achieves high stability but trails in object appearance and 3D layout. SceneRig leads all reported instance-recovery, object-appearance, and 3D-layout metrics (Table 2), with every reconstructed scene passing the stability test.

Qualitative results. Figure 3 compares reconstructions across diverse scenes. For visualization, REST3D and SimFoundry are shown with white support surfaces. In these examples, VIGA alters object geometry, while REST3D and SceneConductor misestimate object scale or placement. SimFoundry also introduces objects absent from the input. SceneRig more faithfully preserves individual objects and their relative positions, including small utensils in cluttered scenes, while reconstructing the surrounding scene. Additional examples are provided in Appendix .

4.3 Ablation Studies

In this section, we evaluate our placement pipeline and the value of the bounded move tool within a physics-enabled agent and compare the influence of VLM backbones and different harnesses.

Physics-grounded object placement. All variants in Table 4 share the same components except object placement. The SAM3D variants retain raw poses, bypassing our metric initialization, settling, and pose refinement. These poses often penetrate or float above supports; settling them for 5 s restores stability but reduces segmentation overlap and 3D placement accuracy. SceneRig’s support-ordered settling and pose refinement improve both while preserving stability. The code-edits-only variant removes Move while retaining Edit, which simulates agent-specified pose changes and returns feedback for agent review. This variant obtains worse object-appearance and 3D-layout scores (Tables 4 and ). Removing Move reduces robot trajectory replay success from 80% to 44% (Appendix , Table ). These results highlight the effectiveness of our physics-grounded tool design.

VLM backbones and reconstruction harnesses. Within SceneRig, replacing Opus 5 with GPT-6 Astra substantially improves appearance but only modestly improves 3D layout (Appendix ). With a shared GPT-6 Astra backbone, SceneRig still achieves better results on most object-centric metrics, more accurate placement, and more stable scenes than VIGA and Codex (Tables 4 and ). These results show that a stronger VLM alone does not ensure accurate and stable object placement: even when all methods use the same stronger backbone, SceneRig still achieves more accurate placement and better physical stability.

5 Robotics Applications

We assess SceneRig with real-to-sim policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay. We compare with SimFoundry, which reconstructs the source-view camera and accounts for physical stability; REST3D’s exported scenes do not retain a calibrated source camera, while VIGA and SceneConductor omit physical simulation. For each episode, both methods reconstruct the scene from an armless head-camera image using its metric depth and calibrated intrinsics instead of monocular estimates. Scenes are registered to the robot using the calibrated head-camera pose.

5.1 Real-to-Sim Policy Evaluation

Setup. We evaluate finetuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} [pi05] and LingBot-VLA 2.0 [lingbotvla2] on five tabletop tasks, using separate sets of 50 real episodes per policy (10 episodes per task, 100 episodes in total). Both reconstructions of each episode run the policy checkpoint used on the real robot, sharing simulator, calibration, and global simulation settings. We report success rates, episode-level agreement, and Cohen’s κ\kappa for each policy. Pearson’s rr is computed both within each policy across five tasks and across all ten policy–task pairs. Details are provided in Appendix .

SceneRig better predicts real-robot outcomes. Simulated outcomes match real ones in 69% of episodes with SceneRig versus 54% with SimFoundry (Tables 6 and ), a significant paired difference (McNemar p=0.017p=0.017), and SceneRig’s Cohen’s κ\kappa exceeds SimFoundry’s by 0.29 (95% CI [0.08, 0.50]). Across ten policy–task pairs, real and simulated success rates correlate at r=0.92r=0.92 with SceneRig and 0.840.84 with SimFoundry, with mean maximum rank violations (MMRV) [li2024simpler] of 0.04 and 0.11 (Figure 4; Table ).

5.2 Open-Loop Trajectory Replay

Setup. We collect and evaluate 25 successful teleoperated demonstrations, five per task. Both SceneRig’s and SimFoundry’s reconstructions of each episode are imported into Isaac Sim with the calibrated bimanual robot. Controllers track the measured joint trajectory and gripper commands from the recorded initial configuration, without policy queries or trajectory adaptation. Commands, calibration, gains, and physics settings are shared (Appendix ).

SceneRig more reliably supports open-loop trajectory replay. SceneRig successfully replays 20/25 demonstrations, versus 9/25 for SimFoundry, with higher success on every task (Table 5); it succeeds on every demonstration that SimFoundry replays successfully (exact McNemar p=0.001p=0.001). SimFoundry fails due to missing objects, misplaced containers, and geometry that obstructs the robot. In Figure , its fused apple–plate mesh lifts the plate when the apple is grasped, while SceneRig preserves separate objects and supports the recorded manipulation.

6 \parDiscussion

Conclusions. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that reconstructs simulation-ready scenes from single images. Its modular harness equips agents with geometric and physical tools to refine object placement through edit-and-validate loops. Across diverse tabletop scenes, SceneRig improves visual fidelity and placement accuracy while maintaining physical stability. Its scenes better predict real-world policy outcomes and more reliably reproduce recorded manipulations. These results offer a path to scaling robot policy evaluation by bringing real workspaces into simulation.

Limitations and future work. Although SceneRig accurately places objects in tabletop scenes, complex room scenes remain challenging due to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and frequent contacts. SAM3D’s lack of PBR materials limits photorealism, and our current representation treats each reconstructed object as a single rigid body and does not recover joint structures or deformation. Future work will explore improved depth estimation and image-to-3D models.
