Appendix A \parSupplementary Material Overview

This supplementary material provides implementation details, evaluation protocols, and additional results for SceneRig. Section Appendix B \parAdditional Implementation Details describes relational perception, object initialization and support-ordered settling, agentic scene construction, object pose refinement, implementation settings, and simulator export. Section Appendix C \parAdditional Experimental Details details baseline implementation and metric definitions, as well as the protocols for real-to-sim policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay. Section Appendix D \parAdditional Experiments presents ablation studies on pose/physics modules, VLM backbones, and harness comparisons, including the direct Codex baseline with GPT-6 Astra, and additional qualitative examples. Code is available at https://github.com/Red-Fairy/SceneRig.

Appendix B \parAdditional Implementation Details

This appendix expands the perception, initialization, and refinement procedures in Sections –. Figures B.1 \parRelational perception and mask recovery, B.3 \parAgentic scene construction, and B.4 \parPhysics-Grounded Pose Refinement summarize relational perception, agentic scene construction, and the pose-refinement loop, respectively. We use the entity IDs and graph notation defined in Section throughout. The descriptions below distinguish model predictions, deterministic tests, and fallbacks. Tables B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export and B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export collect the model roles and implementation defaults.

B.1 \parRelational perception and mask recovery

Scene routing and entity parsing. A routing VLM first classifies the image as a room, a close-up showing a table, or a tabletop close-up. The effective route selects the proposer/verifier prompt pair for support construction and connectivity filtering.

A VLM call then groups entities by category. Each category record contains a short detector-friendly noun, up to three synonyms, and a list of instances. For example, a single mug record can contain a white mug at the front and a blue mug behind it. Each instance has its own description, type (movable object or root surface), and proposed direct support. Attributes and relative locations belong in the instance description, not in the category name. Category names are normalized and duplicate category records are consolidated. The parsing pipeline assigns category-local IDs such as mug#

0 and mug#

1; later recovery steps preserve surviving IDs and allocate new ones for additional instances. Root-surface categories are recognized by their head noun, such as table, wall, floor, or counter. The proposer also emits relations among these surfaces, such as a wall behind a table.

The routing distinction between a tabletop close-up and a view of the table’s body or base determines whether the main support needs only a slab or connected structure beneath it. The ordinary close-up path focuses on the main support and its objects, excluding people and objects on unrelated surfaces. An optional room-scale mode instead treats the floor as a root and furniture as objects. Containers remain objects, with their contents linked to the container as their direct support. Bounding walls receive separate root IDs. Following the proposed support chains identifies the root holding the most objects as the main support. Category grouping shares detection work; it does not assume that all instances have equal physical size.

Point-guided mask selection. MolmoPoint [7] localizes each instance from its description, including root surfaces. SAM3 [3] produces a full-image mask pool for each category; instances of that category share the pool but select masks using their own points. Selection starts with the smallest mask containing the point, then prefers a larger candidate if it contains at least 80%80\%\par of that mask. Partially overlapping instances remain separate. Synonym pools are computed as needed and cached. The recovery ladder proceeds from full-image text prompts, to text prompts on a point-centered crop, to point-prompted SAM3 with all of the instance’s localized points as foreground prompts. Crops initially span one third of the image width and height. A mask cut by an internal crop boundary triggers a larger, two-thirds crop. Root surfaces skip cropping because a local crop can lose their full extent.

Selection is instance-aware. A candidate covering three or more distinct object points is rejected as a merged-object mask; declared support children are excluded from this test. For a singleton category, compatible fragments near the localization point can be joined, and a substantially larger synonym mask can replace a detected part with the whole object. Point prompting normally requires SAM3’s predicted IoU to reach 0.60.6. If single-point prompting returns plausible masks with more than a twofold area difference, a VLM selects the intended object extent instead of comparing confidence scores across these scales; this scale-adjudicated choice bypasses the confidence floor. Roots have a more permissive final fallback: a nearby point-to-mask match is allowed, and a largest-mask choice is used only when localization returns no point. Root point-prompt masks are not subject to the object confidence floor. Each accepted mask records its recovery tier. Instances that exhaust the ladder without a usable mask enter the dropped list with a reason.

Inventory and overlap checks. Object-level checks target missed instances in repeated categories, such as masking only two of three mugs, and objects split across masks, such as a monitor separated into its base and screen. These checks reconcile duplicate assignments and overlaps.

Two instance descriptions can localize the same object. When this causes a duplicate or failed assignment, MolmoPoint gets one retry on an image with already claimed instances of that category crossed out. SAM3 still segments the original image. For categories initially containing multiple objects, unused masks in the category/synonym pools trigger a plural localization query, such as “all the mugs.” A new instance is accepted only when a point from the plural query falls inside a distinct unclaimed SAM3 mask and the mask passes the overlap checks against claimed objects; a VLM supplies its description. Roots are excluded. An initially singleton category is recounted only when its mask combines multiple instances: distinct SAM3 members must each occupy 88–92%92\%\par of its area, lie at least 80%80\%\par inside it, and together cover at least 70%70\%\par of it. MolmoPoint must localize at least two members with a plural query. One member retains the original ID; the others enter the same unclaimed-mask acceptance procedure.

High-overlap masks are first deduplicated by entity type (IoU >0.7>0.7 or containment >0.8>0.8). Cross-category containment is deferred because it may represent a vessel and its contents. For touching object masks, the merge cascade first joins high-overlap duplicates at IoU ≥0.45\geq 0.45, except deferred containment pairs, which require VLM review. Below this threshold, same-category pairs are never merged. Cross-category pairs with IoU 0.250.25–0.450.45 are sent to a VLM; other touching pairs are skipped. Mere contact does not imply one object. The VLM sees an unmarked crop and a red/blue mask overlay. Accepted merges union the masks, preserve the survivor’s ID, and redirect support references. Containment is the fraction of the smaller mask covered by the larger. When over 80%80\%\par of a smaller, cross-category object is embedded in a larger mask, its pixels are removed from the larger mask unless this would remove over half of that mask. This carving runs before occlusion completion; legitimate overlap between completed masks is not carved away afterward.

Object components containing their localization points are retained. A fragment of at least 50 pixels can be restored if it reconnects through an occluder’s mask, contains no other object’s point, and overlaps other objects by at most 10%10\%\par of its area.

Root-surface verification. A separate VLM receives the original image, a color-coded root-mask overlay labeled with IDs, and the root descriptions and proposed relations. It corrects the relations and describes missing surfaces. It can add a root by description without rerunning segmentation, but cannot add, remove, or modify movable objects. Initially unsegmentable roots are dropped; this review can reintroduce missing surfaces as description-only roots in ℛ\mathcal{R\par} for visual construction.

Occlusion completion. Preprocessing invokes generative resegmentation after segmentation; its per-instance checks determine whether an image edit or mask recovery is needed. Mask pairs with at least 20 overlapping pixels after three-pixel dilation are possible occluder–target pairs. A VLM uses their image crops and depth-order evidence to identify the foreground object. A separate crop check for each instance estimates visibility and frame truncation and identifies missing structural parts, such as a handle or base. These judgments feed a deterministic recovery policy. Self-occlusion is not a missing external part. A supporting ancestor will not be treated as an occluder of its descendant. Completion is considered for a missing structural part, visibility below 75%75\%\par, or an overlap-separation loss of at least 150 pixels or 3%3\%\par of the target mask.

We apply LanPaint [57] with Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 [33] to remove the occluder and its support descendants. The edit mask is their union, dilated by 12 pixels; the prompt names the objects to remove and the target to reveal. SAM3 resegments the edited image using a part-aware description, the category, the original localization point, and finally synonyms. Candidate masks must have IoU at least 0.250.25 with the original target or reconnect a missing part within a 10-pixel dilation of it; adjacent-part unions cannot exceed eight times the original area. Sibling masks are excluded. If a candidate covers over 80%80\%\par of a removed foreign object’s footprint, that footprint is clipped outside the original target mask. Removed objects in the target’s support subtree are exempt. The chosen mask must grow by more than 2%2\%\par. When overlap carving alone triggers recovery, failed resegmentation can instead use the union of the original target and removed footprints. Other failures retain the original evidence. If only a structural part was missed, resegmentation uses the original image without an edit.

A VLM audits newly generated candidates using aligned before/after RGB images and masked cutouts. It checks target identity and count and mask fidelity; edited images additionally require preserved observed geometry and plausible completion, with occluder removal checked when applicable. All applicable checks must pass; rejection, uncertainty, or an unavailable judgment retains the original evidence. This audit also applies to the union fallback and border completion. Older cached completions without an audit may be reused, but are explicitly marked unverified.

RGB completion alone would leave the removed object’s depth in the newly revealed region. We therefore invalidate depth in the edit hole and pass the edited RGB image, remaining MoGe-2 depth, and camera intrinsics to LingBot-Depth [39]. Its completed metric points support mesh reconstruction and placement. Original masks, depth, and camera records are retained separately, and failed image or depth completion falls back to the available original evidence.

A separate border-completion branch handles masks reaching within three pixels of exactly one left or right image edge. Completion requires either a VLM estimate of at least 10%10\%\par beyond-frame extent or edge contact in at least 85%85\%\par of the rows within the mask’s bounding box. Eligible cases receive a 25%25\%\par canvas extension on that side, followed by LanPaint/Qwen outpainting and LingBot depth completion. Occluder removal, when needed, is a separate edit. Padding shifts the camera’s principal point but does not change its physical viewpoint. The extended image helps reconstruct the complete asset; source-view registration still uses the original image domain. This branch does not extrapolate arbitrary top, bottom, or two-sided truncations.

Post-completion cleanup. After completion, a further VLM pass checks whether nearby point-prompted detections are parts of one physical assembly, such as a stand and its supported device. Candidate masks must touch or lie within a small dilation of one another; proximity alone does not justify merging them. The VLM must identify them as parts of the same object. Merges update support references as well as masks. Objects without a usable mask are removed before the final inventory is fixed, with their records and reasons retained for inspection.

After completion and component merging, a connectivity check filters objects assigned directly to masked roots. An object must connect to its support, either directly or through accepted objects sharing that support, within approximately 3%3\%\par of the image’s shorter dimension. Disconnected objects are removed before fixing the inventory. The check uses completed masks when available, except for border completion, whose extended canvas requires the original in-frame mask. Objects supported by other objects or unmasked roots are exempt from this check.

B.2 \parMetric initialization and support-ordered settling

Metric frame and relation validation. MoGe-2 [42] estimates metric depth, camera intrinsics, normals, and a dense point map. A RANSAC fit to the main support estimates the upward direction. The fit starts from the localized support component and includes compatible coplanar fragments. A direction-consensus step also considers planar support components and planes on directly supported objects, reducing the effect of a contaminated support mask. The mean predicted support normal is a fallback when a point-based fit is unreliable. Small estimated camera rolls below 2.5∘2.5^{\circ} are removed in the monocular path; calibrated depth inputs retain their measured roll.

For an upward unit vector uu and a support-plane point p0p_{0}, the canonical transform satisfies

Rg​u=ez,pcan=Rg​p+tg,tg=(0,0,−ez⊤​Rg​p0)⊤.R_{g}u=e_{z},\qquad p^{\mathrm{can\par}}=R_{g}p+t_{g},\qquad t_{g}=(0,0,-e_{z}^{\top}R_{g}p_{0})^{\top}.

Thus gravity is along −z-z and the main support lies at z=0z=0. The same transform is applied to the camera. If the declared main support has no usable mask, another supported horizontal root is considered; if none is measurable, a fallback level ground is placed below the observed object bases. These fallback choices are recorded rather than treated as measured support planes.

Root-plane reliability depends on both RANSAC inliers and image coverage, so a narrow wall sliver cannot provide a strong orientation constraint. Reliable near-horizontal normals are leveled and near-vertical walls are made plumb. Ambiguous or unmeasurable planes remain visual construction tasks, not grounds for deleting a root.

Root relations distinguish flush support–wall contact (against), a joined horizontal/vertical pair (perpendicular), two walls meeting at a vertical edge (corner), and a lower surface supporting the full base of an upper structure (under). We then verify VLM-estimated relationships via monocular geometry. Confirmed relations become required construction constraints; uncertain or conflicting relations remain advisory, and rejected ones are not enforced. The graph stores this status and its evidence along with EsupE_{\mathrm{sup\par}} and EsurfE_{\mathrm{surf\par}}. Every support ID must resolve to an entity, parent and child records must agree, and support cycles are forbidden.

Object assets and physical properties. SAM3D [6] reconstructs a textured mesh from the full-frame image and the instance mask. Its predicted orientation is transformed into the gravity-aligned frame without reflection. The mesh is centered at the metric position and uniformly scaled by the depth-projected 3D points of that object after outlier filtering. Both the posed mesh and an unposed canonical copy are saved; the latter supplies an alternative upright orientation during settling. Materials are rendered double-sided to avoid transparent-looking open mesh shells.

Following SceneSmith [32], a VLM estimates material and mass from metric dimensions, sealed mesh volume, six mesh renders (four sides, top, and bottom), and a marked crop showing the object in the input image. Friction comes from a material lookup table, not an unconstrained numerical VLM prediction. An implied density above three times the material density triggers one reconsideration; a still-excessive estimate is clamped. Low implied density is only flagged because hollow objects are legitimate. Missing estimates use the documented density and friction defaults. An estimate made at box dimensions bo0b_{o}^{0} is rescaled to current dimensions bob_{o} by

mophys=mo0​∏j=13bo,jbo,j0.m_{o}^{\mathrm{phys\par}}=m_{o}^{0}\prod_{j=1}^{3}\frac{b_{o,j}\par}{b_{o,j}^{0}\par}.

This gives the cubic law under uniform scaling. Physical-property overrides retain consistent mass, center-of-mass, and inertia records.

Nearby-view references. We combine SHARP [27] with GPT-Image-2 [30] to render nearby views. SHARP predicts a 3D Gaussian representation once from the input image, using the estimated focal length. We render it at four source-camera offsets: (+30∘,0)(+30^{\circ},0), (−30∘,0)(-30^{\circ},0), (0,+15∘)(0,+15^{\circ}), and (0,−15∘)(0,-15^{\circ}) in azimuth and elevation. The orbit uses the estimated gravity direction and normally pivots about the source viewing axis’s intersection with the main-support plane. A grazing or implausibly distant intersection falls back to the centroid of all objects’ positions projected onto the support plane.

SHARP renders can contain holes, haze, or stretched edges. Thus, we use GPT-Image-2 to edit each rendered image with instructions to repair these artifacts while preserving clear content and viewpoint. This is a mask-free edit of the rendered view, not a text-only request for a new angle and not a paired input-photo edit. We do not composite original pixels back into the generated result. To detect content drift, pixels with SHARP alpha below 0.80.8, dilated by 1%1\%\par of the image’s long edge, are excluded from a comparison of raw and edited RGB. The edit is rejected if the mean absolute difference over the remaining observed pixels exceeds 25/25525/255, after resizing it to the raw render’s resolution. Up to three edit attempts are allowed. An unsuccessful view may retain its raw render for diagnosis but is not exposed as a trusted reference.

If SHARP fails, the fallback splats MoGe-2 points into the same cameras and uses masked GPT-Image-2 editing to fill disocclusions. Generated images are visual guidance, not measured ground truth, and their hidden content may be inaccurate. Agents receive the requested render/reference pair on demand; the source-view reference is always the original photograph. The lighting stage uses only that real source view, since generated illumination is not reliable evidence for lighting estimation.

Support-ordered settling. CoACD [44] converts each mesh into compound convex collision shapes. Supports and containers receive finer decomposition to preserve interior cavities. The validated decomposition is reused during pose refinement and export when the mesh differs only by a recoverable transform; geometry changes trigger rebuilding. A persistent PhysX scene processes objects in parent-before-child order under EsupE_{\mathrm{sup\par}}, with larger footprints prioritized where dependencies permit. This order applies to initial placement, not the pose agent’s investigation sequence. Temporary root slabs provide support until the initialization agent builds root geometry.

Each object is first dropped against its support context, then against the already placed scene. It is released 2 mm above collision-free contact and simulated with all six rigid-body degrees of freedom. For a non-rollable object, excessive tilt triggers a recovery ladder: try the canonical upright mesh orientation, then a guarded physical-property adjustment. The adjustment can flatten a narrow collider base band, move or lower the center of mass, and increase friction and damping, with matching inertia. A sliver-like contact footprint disables this adjustment to avoid manufacturing an implausible balancing pose. If no upright candidate works, the actual fallen resting pose is retained and flagged. Rollable objects instead use horizontal displacement to detect instability; rolling in place is allowed, and center-of-mass stabilization is skipped. Small lateral searches address collisions with neighbors, and a bounded inward nudge can move an object off its support’s rim.

After settling, trimmed iterative closest point (ICP) alignment fits the mesh to the masked metric points. It optimizes horizontal translation, yaw, and uniform scale about the object’s bottom center; the fitted vertical offset is discarded so simulation determines resting height. The correction must reduce point-to-mesh RMS error by at least 20%20\%\par. Scale is fixed for equal-size or otherwise scale-locked assets. ICP is skipped after a successful rim or wrong-support escape, where fitting the original points would undo the rescue. A correction needing more than 3 cm of collision clearance is rejected. Otherwise, another drop tests convergence and class-appropriate stability; failure restores the exact pre-ICP pose. An already fallen object is not rejected merely for retaining that same attitude. Accepted collision shapes remain in the scene for subsequent objects. After all objects are placed, a final joint pass releases every object at once in a single free simulation run to rest; the resulting small drift is baked into the saved poses and recorded per object before the scene is imported into Blender.

B.3 \parAgentic scene construction

Generator–verifier interaction. Each stage pairs a VLM generator, which edits and renders the Blender scene, with a VLM verifier, which compares the render with the reference images. Both receive the allowed edits for that stage, the object and root-surface records 𝒪\mathcal{O\par} and ℛ\mathcal{R\par}, the relation graph GG, and the current Blender scene through a stage-entry snapshot and scene-inspection tools. The snapshot exposes object names, transforms, dimensions, materials, lights, and camera state; the graph supplies stable IDs, supports, descriptions, and root-plane evidence. A stage-specific prompt states which of these quantities may change. The original image remains the visual anchor.

The generator edits scene code, renders the result, and can undo its latest edit. The read-only verifier sees a current render and the generator’s relevant actions and rule evidence. It either approves the stage or returns concrete corrections within the same scope. A retry continues from the shared scene, not a reset scene; initialization also carries forward its construction plan. Feedback from unrelated stages is not repeatedly inserted into the prompt. Budgets bound this loop. Reaching a budget without approval produces a best-effort artifact sent to the subsequent stage. Figure B.3 \parAgentic scene construction shows the shared-scene progression.

Stage-specific edits. The initialization generator constructs root geometry and placement from reliable fitted planes, the reference image, and EsurfE_{\mathrm{surf\par}}. Plane points and normals constrain position and orientation; the photograph determines shape and finite extent. A frame-clipped mask supplies only a lower bound beyond the clipped edge. The main support is level with its top at z=0z=0, but its horizontal position, footprint, and yaw remain adjustable. Walls follow their measured horizontal normal and vertical direction through an orthogonal basis. Roots lacking reliable planes are built from their descriptions and the photograph. A required floor-under-table relation calls for connected legs or a base reaching the floor, rather than placing the floor just beneath the tabletop slab.

Every registered root must be represented. Openings can be cut into a wall, with small frame or glass details attached to that wall. A dedicated root-creation tool can register a genuinely missing architectural wall, and only such runtime-added roots can be removed through the corresponding tool. The agent cannot silently delete a preprocessed root or create duplicate unregistered walls. One auxiliary level ground is allowed when needed. Root collision geometry is static, with predefined friction. Coarse materials and lighting are initialized once before later appearance refinement.

Imported object poses are the trusted starting point. Initialization may translate an object or support stack only through a controlled correction tool, in response to a measured contact defect or a clear position mismatch in paired images. It cannot rotate, resize, remesh, or retexture the object. The correction tool tests object integrity, support, and new or worsened collisions, rolls back a failed correction, and requires another rule check after success. Moving an object merely to compensate for a wrongly built support is disallowed.

The appearance stage changes root materials and textures τr\tau_{r}, including procedural shader detail, roughness, and bump patterns, while keeping geometry and object assets fixed. The illumination stage changes lights, world illumination, exposure, and view-transform settings, not materials or layout. It compares only source-view renders with the input image. The source camera stays fixed; alternate views use rendering tools rather than camera edits.

Rule checks and visual feedback. As a special tool for the initialization stage only, the read-only check_rules tool evaluates three levels in sequence. Structure checks verify imported-object integrity, registered-root coverage, main-support geometry, top height, and required structural relations. Pose checks compare root silhouettes with the reference masks and verify that all objects rest on their supports. Contact checks detect penetration, floating objects, and violated surface relations. Advisory relations do not acquire the force of required constraints. The report identifies the first failing level and its affected entities; later levels are not evaluated and must not be assumed to pass.

The initialization generator revises the scene and reruns the tool after edits. Its voluntary completion requires a current pass and verifier approval. For ambiguous or tiny wall masks, an explicit visibility exception can waive an unreliable mask comparison, but not the requirement to build the root. Passing numerical rules establishes a minimum geometric standard, not visual faithfulness: the verifier still judges table edges, wall placement, gaps, and visible structure. Appearance and lighting have their own visual verifiers without this initialization rule ladder. Their feedback targets root-surface appearance and source-view lighting, respectively.

B.4 \parPhysics-Grounded Pose Refinement

Object investigation. Pose refinement uses one continuous VLM session, without an external verifier or a fresh-memory retry. The agent interprets visual evidence and selects tools for geometric measurement, pose search, and simulation. Scene-rendering tools provide source, nearby, and bird’s-eye views. The investigation tool returns paired, labeled photo/render crops for one object or a small spatially adjacent group. Small objects are inspected alone or in pairs so that their directional features remain visible. Investigation makes only the listed IDs eligible for bounded moves; the next investigation replaces that set, while code edits and undo clear it.

The Investigate tool reports silhouette overlap and separate evidence for displacement, projected size, fine yaw, and front–back orientation. Comparing raw and centroid-aligned overlap helps detect displacement. Projected size compares radial mask extents, or major-axis extents for elongated objects; a large position error or incompatible aspect ratios suppress an unreliable size suggestion. Yaw is measured from silhouette principal axes only when the axis is sufficiently distinctive. Missing evidence means unmeasured, not correct. The agent checks the paired crops and distinguishes a depth error from a true size error before resizing.

Front–back evidence compares the current crop and a 180∘180^{\circ} yaw-flipped render with the photograph using DINOv2 [31] patch features. Weak and strong reversal margins are reported separately; nearly tied or unavailable features do not establish an orientation. For elongated objects, a significant fine-yaw error postpones the flip suggestion until comparable crops are available. When an accepted occlusion-completed reference exists, a known foreground object resting on the target can be hidden in the render and paired with its removal-edited reference. Uncertain neighbors and objects being investigated together remain visible.

Bounded candidate search. The agent selects an object and a move aspect aa from six choices: horizontal translation along xx, along yy, or jointly in x​yxy; uniform scaling; yaw adjustment; or a 180∘180^{\circ} yaw flip. The flip follows the special procedure described below. For routine bounded moves, the agent does not specify the adjustment magnitude or search direction. The Move tool evaluates a coarse candidate set and then finer candidates around the winner. Translation step sizes are proportional to object size, so larger objects are tested with larger shifts. For joint xx–yy moves, the tool compares the rendered object mask with the reference mask and uses their offset to propose a translation. Scale and yaw searches can similarly use measured size and orientation differences to propose candidates. Before rendering each candidate, the tool resolves overlap with the support and adjusts the object’s height to place it on the geometry below. These geometric placement operations do not run a physics simulation. Candidates are ranked using the alignment scores below; only the selected candidate proceeds to physical settling and acceptance checks.

Aspect-specific alignment scores. Let mom_{o} be the reference mask and m^o​(X)\widehat{m}_{o}(X) the rendered silhouette of object oo at transform XX. We write IoUo⁡(X)=IoU⁡(m^o​(X),mo)\operatorname{IoU\par}_{o}(X)=\operatorname{IoU\par}(\widehat{m}_{o}(X),m_{o}); cIoUo⁡(X)\operatorname{cIoU\par}_{o}(X) aligns the masks’ area-weighted centroids before comparison. Both use coverage-weighted masks, preserving fractional alpha values and thin structures. The score for aspect aa is

Ao(a)​(X)={IoUo⁡(X)−0.4​Do​(X)−0.3​Qo​(X),a=translation,cIoUo⁡(X)−0.4​Do​(X)−0.3​Qo​(X),a=scale,cIoUo⁡(X)+0.2​Fo​(X),a=yaw.A_{o}^{(a)}(X)=\begin{cases}\par\textstyle\operatorname{IoU\par}_{o}(X)-0.4D_{o}(X)-0.3Q_{o}(X),&a=\text{translation\par},\\ \par\par\textstyle\operatorname{cIoU\par}_{o}(X)-0.4D_{o}(X)-0.3Q_{o}(X),&a=\text{scale\par},\\ \par\par\textstyle\operatorname{cIoU\par}_{o}(X)+0.2F_{o}(X),&a=\text{yaw\par}.\end{cases}

Here, Do​(X)=|do​(X)−doref|/|doref|D_{o}(X)=|d_{o}(X)-d_{o}^{\mathrm{ref\par}}|/|d_{o}^{\mathrm{ref\par}}| measures relative depth error. do​(X)d_{o}(X) is the depth of the object’s center after the candidate translation, and dorefd_{o}^{\mathrm{ref\par}} is the median depth of the masked points of that object. The size penalty Qo​(X)=||m^o​(X)|/|mo|−1|Q_{o}(X)=\left|\par\sqrt{|\widehat{m}_{o}(X)|/|m_{o}|}-1\right|\par compares projected mask areas. Centering the masks for scale and yaw reduces interference from translation errors; depth and projected size constrain translation and scale. Yaw additionally uses appearance to distinguish orientations with similar silhouettes. Specifically,

Fo​(X)=1|𝒫o|​∑p∈𝒫ofprender​(X)⊤​fpphoto‖fprender​(X)‖2​‖fpphoto‖2,F_{o}(X)=\frac{1\par}{|\mathcal{P\par}_{o}|\par}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P\par}_{o}}\frac{f_{p}^{\mathrm{render\par}}(X)^{\top}f_{p}^{\mathrm{photo\par}}\par}{\|f_{p}^{\mathrm{render\par}}(X)\|_{2}\|f_{p}^{\mathrm{photo\par}}\|_{2}\par},

where fpf_{p} is a DINOv2 ViT-S/14 patch token from an RGB object crop and 𝒫o\mathcal{P\par}_{o} indexes reference-foreground patches in matched-size crops. If no foreground patch survives downsampling, the full patch grid is used. The scoring window is the reference mask’s box with 25%25\%\par padding, and the isolated render is composited on neutral gray. The front–back comparison crops each object to its own box on white and resizes to 224×224224\times 224, reducing sensitivity to position and scale. Without DINOv2 features, yaw uses silhouette scoring and supplies no appearance evidence for orientation.

Simulation and acceptance. Let XoX_{o} be the pre-edit transform, Xo′X^{\prime}_{o} the proposal tested for acceptance after any reduction to a feasible fraction, and X^o\widehat{X}_{o} its simulated resting pose. The post-settling score A~o(a)​(X^o)\widetilde{A}_{o}^{(a)}(\widehat{X}_{o}) recomputes rendered terms while holding the tested proposal’s depth penalty fixed. Let PoP_{o} indicate that the applicable proposal-level yaw check and post-settling physical checks pass. For routine bounded moves, the update is

Xo←{X^o,Ao(a)​(Xo′)−Ao(a)​(Xo)≥ϵa,Po=1,A~o(a)(X^o)≥Ao(a)(Xo),Xo,otherwise.X_{o}\leftarrow\begin{cases}\par\textstyle\widehat{X}_{o},&\begin{aligned} \par\hfil\displaystyle&A_{o}^{(a)}(X^{\prime}_{o})-A_{o}^{(a)}(X_{o})\geq\epsilon_{a},\\ \par\par\hfil\displaystyle&P_{o}=1,\quad\widetilde{A}_{o}^{(a)}(\widehat{X}_{o})\geq A_{o}^{(a)}(X_{o}),\end{aligned}\\[2.0pt] \par\par\textstyle X_{o},&\text{otherwise\par}.\end{cases}

The aspect-specific threshold ϵa\epsilon_{a} suppresses small proposed gains; after settling, retaining the baseline score is sufficient. Table B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export lists the gain and physical thresholds. Collision checks compare pre- and post-edit penetration, rejecting substantial new or worsened overlap; pre-existing overlap is still subject to the final whole-scene rule gate. Non-rollable objects are checked for capsize, while rollable objects are checked for excessive horizontal drift.

A failed candidate can be reduced to a smaller feasible fraction, which must again clear the gain threshold before simulation. Reliable yaw evidence adds an improvement test on the selected proposal, with a small noise tolerance. If appearance features become unavailable during rescoring, their term is removed from both scores in the post-settling comparison. Rejection restores all affected transforms, including those of supported objects.

Support propagation and exceptional edits. Equation (B.4 \parPhysics-Grounded Pose Refinement) applies to routine bounded searches. The 180∘180^{\circ} flip is a special semantic correction: it need not improve IoU, but is physically tested and must be followed immediately by a fresh paired investigation or undo. A retained or undone applied flip consumes its one-shot allowance; one physically rejected attempt can be retried.

When moving a support parent, the Move tool compares leaving children in place with carrying them. Children follow if the free-child simulation would topple them or if carrying improves the group’s mean overlap. A resize instead settles the resized parent and then reseats its children and contact-dependent neighbors.

When bounded moves repeatedly fail or cannot express a correction, the code-edit tool Edit allows direct layout changes, including coordinated edits. The scene-code editing tool detects changed objects, resolves initial overlaps, and settles affected supports before their dependents in simulation. It then returns the post-simulation render and physical diagnostics for the agent to decide whether to retain or undo the simulated result. Automatic alignment and physical acceptance checks govern bounded moves; the agent decides whether to retain simulated code edits. If the required simulation fails to execute, the raw edit is rolled back. Undo restores the pre-edit scene snapshot rather than using approximate inverse transforms.

Context management and prompt caching. The agent retains the initial instructions, target image, and stage-entry scene snapshot. Recent rounds retain their full text, while older rounds are compressed in blocks of four into a chronological log, normally leaving five to eight recent rounds. The log preserves actions, scores, acceptance/rejection, and undo outcomes, but removes old images and stale pose suggestions. A compression boundary is moved backward if it would separate an edit from its undo, so the recent window can occasionally grow beyond eight rounds.

Images are also aged within the visible history. Superseded full-scene renders, alternate views, and crop messages become text references to their saved artifacts; paired crop/reference messages are retained or removed together. Duplicate source photographs need not be reattached because the initial target remains protected. Aging occurs at the same block boundaries, not on every round, so it does not continually rewrite the prompt prefix. The full stored history remains intact; compression changes only what is sent to the VLM. The shorter initialization, appearance, and lighting conversations use append-only history rather than this pose-specific sliding window.

A per-object state table is rebuilt from the full interaction history. It records the latest measured scores, completed or pending follow-up checks, tool-use counts, rejected aspects, and exhausted budgets. The table and remaining-round budget sit after the cache breakpoint, at the changing end of the prompt. Their updates therefore preserve the reusable prefix. Block-aligned compression and image aging allow prompt-cache hits across consecutive calls without freezing the current object state. Figure B.4 \parPhysics-Grounded Pose Refinement illustrates this mechanism.

Across all 80 benchmark scenes, 84.1%

of pose-refinement input tokens are cache reads, measured over 2,112 logged calls. We divide summed cache-read tokens by total input tokens, including uncached inputs and cache writes in the denominator and excluding output tokens.

Completion and export. The completion tool, End, first checks that every retained object has been investigated. A coverage failure stops this check before the expensive penetration pass, so it does not imply collision clearance. Once coverage passes, unresolved penetration must be corrected, and any post-flip follow-up must be complete. Voluntary completion and a current rule pass are both required. A budget-limited session is explicitly marked incomplete.

After refinement, one joint gravity simulation releases all objects together. Its resulting transforms are baked into the saved Blender scene; no object is pinned merely to conceal a final topple. Non-convergence, large drift, or toppling is recorded as a warning, and does not by itself establish dynamic simulation readiness. Appendix B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export details USD conversion and its separate readiness check.

B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export

Model roles and execution settings. Table B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export lists the models used in our system and their roles. In the backbone comparison (Table D.1 \parAblation Studies), we switch all configurable VLM roles to the selected backbone, including preprocessing, physical-property estimation, scene-construction generators and verifiers, and pose refinement. Table B.5 \parImplementation settings and simulator export reports implementation defaults, which can be overridden by a run configuration.

Simulator Export. USD conversion is a separate step after Blender reconstruction. It bakes procedural materials and transfers meshes, textures, lights, and camera state, then assigns collision geometry and physical properties. An identity map links each pipeline object to its USD primitive, accounting for name sanitization. Missing, ambiguous, or nested object identities fail conversion rather than losing bodies. Mass and inertia are adjusted consistently for the exported geometry. A simulator-side verification checks the exact object inventory, dynamic versus kinematic state, support contact, convergence, translation and rotation drift, and final velocities. Reconstruction completion, conversion success, and dynamic readiness are recorded separately.

Appendix C \parAdditional Experimental Details

C.1 \parBaseline implementation details

We adapt the baseline implementations to the same single-image benchmark. Each method retains its reconstruction pipeline and scene representation; method-specific adapters expose the reconstructed objects and evaluation renders. Below we describe these adaptations and, in particular, how a source camera and a nearby evaluation camera are obtained.

VIGA. We use VIGA’s static-scene configuration with SAM-based segmentation and SAM3D asset initialization, followed by iterative Blender code generation, rendering, and verifier feedback. To support object-centric evaluation and simulation, we augment the generator’s system prompt with a simple object-grouping contract (one parent per movable object with every part beneath it, one parent for the static environment, no loose top-level meshes), and after every code execution the tool result lists the meshes that are not yet grouped, so the agent can repair them before it stops. We use a 20-round generator budget with medium reasoning effort for every backbone; the same VLM also names the segmented objects. Grouping changes neither the renderer nor the assets, and the agent complied in every scene. Intermediate renders preserve the input aspect ratio with a 512-pixel long edge. For evaluation, we select the latest numbered render directory containing a rendered frame and load its saved Blender scene. We select the main camera by name, falling back to the camera named Camera and then an available camera, and retain its saved pose and intrinsics. This avoids using a diagnostic camera left active. Evaluation renders use the input-image dimensions.

SceneConductor. We run the three-stage pipeline: mask review and merging, SAM3D asset generation and GALP layout initialization; environment construction; and relation-guided scene refinement, including refinement of selected object groups in isolated subscenes. Its source camera uses GALP’s predicted focal length and orientation in the camera-centered reconstruction frame, with the pipeline’s coordinate-convention correction. We render the final scene at the input-image dimensions, preserving its aspect ratio instead of using the default fixed-size diagnostic views. Walls that obstruct the evaluation camera are hidden from camera rays. The nearby-view adapter also uses a gray world background with unit-strength ambient illumination.

SimFoundry. We use the pipeline’s single-image mode: the input is supplied as one RGB frame, with a repeated-frame video only to satisfy the video input interface. Reconstruction uses DA3 depth and camera estimates, support-plane alignment, object extraction and image cleanup, Hunyuan3D asset generation, FoundationPose refinement, and physics preparation and settling before OmniGibson scene assembly. The source camera combines the estimated intrinsics with the camera-to-world transform from support-plane alignment. The single-image configuration uses the simulator’s planar support surface. Pairwise evaluation renders use OmniGibson at a 1536-pixel long edge with the input aspect ratio; the simulator’s added robot is hidden.

REST3D and source-camera recovery. We evaluate REST3D’s final object reconstruction after its scene assembly and stabilization stages. Its exported scene does not retain a calibrated source camera, so our evaluation adapter recovers an approximate camera from the input image and the reconstruction intermediates. We rerun the same MoGe model used by its asset pipeline to estimate image intrinsics. To recover the pose, we fit the reconstructed raw floor/carpet geometry with a plane, use its normal to recover the pipeline’s up-axis alignment, and propagate the raw camera origin, forward direction, and up direction through that alignment. We then apply the support-plane height shift and the conversion from the pipeline’s YY-up frame to the evaluation ZZ-up frame. This recovery is approximate because REST3D’s subsequent per-object grounding and stabilization are not a single rigid scene transform. The camera is derived geometrically from these intermediates, without selecting it by render similarity or using a ground-truth simulator camera. The final meshes are converted to USD with vertex colors retained and rendered in Isaac Sim at the input resolution, using the recovered horizontal focal length, square pixels, and a centered principal point. A synthetic support slab is added because the raw floor reference is omitted from the final object export. For the shared stability test, REST3D’s reconstructed tables and desks and its one wall-mounted object are static colliders; every other REST3D mesh is a dynamic rigid body on the support slab.

SAM3D object baseline. This comparison shares SceneRig’s segmentation and generated object assets. We retain SAM3D’s predicted rotation, translation, and scale, applying only the camera-coordinate conversion and the shared gravity alignment to place them in the scene frame. We bypass SceneRig’s depth-based recentering and rescaling, registration, settling, and subsequent object-pose refinement. For rendering, these raw-pose assets replace the objects in SceneRig’s final scene while retaining its source camera, support surfaces, walls, and lighting. Thus this is an object-reconstruction and placement baseline with shared scene context.

Source and nearby view selection. Source-view metrics use the camera supplied or recovered for each method as described above. For pairwise judging, we render a nearby view by rotating the source camera position cc by +30∘+30^{\circ} around a pivot pp and the reconstruction’s vertical axis:

cnear=p+Rz​(30∘)​(c−p).c_{\mathrm{near\par}}=p+R_{z}(30^{\circ})(c-p).

The focal length and the camera’s height and distance relative to pp are preserved. Each nearby view is thus a corresponding viewpoint change in the reconstruction’s own frame, not a shared ground-truth extrinsic, and is used only for evaluation.

The pivot pp is where the source optical axis meets a horizontal reference plane. REST3D and SimFoundry use the support plane z=0z=0; SceneConductor uses its estimated floor height; VIGA uses the median height of visible mesh bounding-box centers. If the intersection is invalid, REST3D falls back to its scene bounding-box center, SceneConductor to the placed-object centroid, and VIGA to the component-wise median of the visible mesh bounding-box centers (also used when the intersection lies too far outside the scene); the REST3D and SceneConductor fallbacks are projected onto their reference planes. Because each camera is aimed at its pivot, a fixed orbital elevation does not guarantee identical roll, or identical pitch when a fallback pivot is used.

The source and nearby images are presented to the judge at common tile sizes, preserving aspect ratio, together with the original input photograph (Appendix C.3 \parPairwise VLM and physics protocols). Rendering remains method-specific: VIGA and SceneConductor use Blender/Cycles, REST3D uses Isaac Sim, and SimFoundry uses OmniGibson. The scored REST3D and SimFoundry renders use their brown synthetic support surfaces.

C.2 \parBenchmark and metric details

Benchmark composition. The 80-scene benchmark comprises 44 simulator-grounded scenes and 36 additional scenes whose input images consist of 18 real robot workspace images, 6 phone captures, 8 internet images, and 4 AI-generated images.

Image and instance metrics. Full-frame metrics compare the source-camera render with the input image. LPIPS uses AlexNet features; nCLIP is one minus the cosine similarity of CLIP ViT-B/32 image embeddings. The reported PSNR uses raw RGB errors, without fitting an exposure or color correction. Object-only PSNR pools squared errors over ground-truth object pixels, excluding the support table. Object-only SSIM averages the spatial SSIM map over the same pixels.

For object-centric LPIPS and nCLIP, ground-truth instance masks define crop boxes shared by the reference and render. Boxes have 10%10\%\par padding and a minimum side of 64 pixels; objects with fewer than 200 visible pixels are excluded from crop metrics. Within each box, pixels outside the object’s ground-truth mask are set to white in both images, so these metrics score the object without its surroundings. Crop scores are averaged over objects within a scene.

Ground-truth mesh parts are grouped into logical objects before instance evaluation. ARI compares the two instance partitions over all pixels, with background, including the table, treated as one cluster. FG-IoU is the intersection over union between the predicted and ground-truth object foregrounds, each the union of its object pixels with the table excluded. Thus ARI measures partitioning while FG-IoU measures detection coverage: missed, hallucinated, or misplaced objects lower FG-IoU even when the remaining pixels are partitioned consistently. Count MAE is the mean absolute difference between the predicted and ground-truth object counts in the evaluated instance masks. For final-scene evaluation, the predicted count includes only objects visible in the source-view render, rather than all objects stored in the reconstructed scene.

Canonical 3D layout evaluation. Ground-truth and predicted positions are expressed in corresponding canonical frames whose origins are the source viewing axis’s intersections with the support plane. The vertical axis is gravity-up, and the horizontal orientation is fixed by the source-camera direction. If either camera cannot define this intersection, each set instead uses the centroid of all objects’ positions projected onto the support plane. For both predictions and ground truth, object positions are defined by world-space axis-aligned bounding-box centers and then transformed into the canonical frame. All predicted objects contribute to the metric, including unmatched extras. We evaluate object arrangement up to a global scale factor, allowing comparison across reconstruction methods with different scale conventions.

We fit only a global scale. Candidate scales include one and ratios of the two sets’ pairwise-distance quantiles at 2525, 5050, 7575, and 90%90\%\par. Hungarian matching at a 20 cm cutoff ranks candidates first by match count and then by mean matched distance. Up to two least-squares refinements use s=∑ipi⊤​gi/∑i‖pi‖22s=\sum_{i}p_{i}^{\top}g_{i}/\sum_{i}\|p_{i}\|_{2}^{2} for matched predicted and true positions (pi,gi)(p_{i},g_{i}). Refinement requires at least three matches and cannot reduce their count. This scale is shared across all reported cutoffs.

For point sets PP and QQ with m≤nm\leq n elements and n>0n>0, OSPA of order one is

OSPAc⁡(P,Q)=1n​[min⁡∑i=1mπ⁡min⁡(c,‖pi−qπ⁡(i)‖2)+c⁡(n−m)],\operatorname{OSPA\par}_{c}(P,Q)=\frac{1\par}{n\par}\left[\par\min_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\min\!\left(\par c,\|p_{i}-q_{\pi(i)}\|_{2}\right)\par+c(n-m)\right]\par,

where π\pi assigns the smaller set to distinct members of the larger. Two empty sets have zero distance. It penalizes localization error and unmatched objects [36]. We report 5 and 10 cm cutoffs and F1 from a separate 10 cm-threshold assignment on these aligned positions.

C.3 \parPairwise VLM and physics protocols

For pairwise visual evaluation, GPT-5.6-terra and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B [34] compare reconstruction pairs for completeness, layout, and appearance. The nearby evaluation view uses the 30∘30^{\circ} orbit and method-specific camera recovery described in Appendix C.1 \parBaseline implementation details, keeping the camera’s orbital elevation and distance fixed. Each candidate panel shows its source and nearby render, with anonymous labels and uniform tile sizes; the judge also sees the real input photograph. Each pair is presented in both candidate orders. We remove order-inconsistent judgments, give ties half credit, and fit Bradley–Terry scores to summarize pairwise preferences. Half a pseudo-win is added in each direction for every compared method pair to avoid infinite strength estimates for undefeated methods. Scores are centered to have zero mean across methods for each criterion. After excluding comparisons for which either judge is order-inconsistent, the two judges achieve Cohen’s κ=0.87\kappa=0.87. Order-inconsistent verdicts, discarded as above, make up 13–23%

of paired judgments per criterion.

Physical stability is evaluated separately by running each reconstructed scene for 300 PhysX steps at 60 Hz. Displacement is the Euclidean distance between an object’s initial and final position, not accumulated travel along its path. An object passes the stability test if its displacement after 5 s is below 50 mm and its final velocity is zero; a scene passes only if every object passes. The scene-level rate is the fraction of passing scenes, while the object-level rate pools passing objects across scenes.

C.4 \parReal-to-sim policy evaluation protocol

This section details the two policy evaluations in Section . Table reports π0.5\pi_{0.5} and Table C.4 \parReal-to-sim policy evaluation protocol reports LingBot-VLA 2.0; both policies are fine-tuned on the same in-house teleoperation data and evaluated on separate sets of 50 real episodes across the same five tasks: ten episodes per policy–task pair, totaling 100 real episodes. Each episode is evaluated in both reconstruction methods with its corresponding policy checkpoint. The five tasks evaluated are: everything into the bin, fruit on plate, fruits from plate to bowl, marker in cup, and mustard in bin.

Scene export. Each scene is reconstructed by SceneRig (or baseline) from an armless head-camera image and exported to Isaac Sim together with the calibrated camera rig of the station, the episode’s initial arm configuration (reset pose), and the episode’s text instruction. Unlike the RGB-only benchmark of Section , these station scenes provide metric depth: both SceneRig and SimFoundry receive the head camera’s color-aligned depth map, hole-completed with LingBot-Depth [39], together with the calibrated intrinsics, and use it in place of monocular depth estimation. Both methods use their own mass estimates for objects, and the friction coefficient is derived from the estimated material; contacts use the larger friction coefficient of the two bodies. The gripper fingertips use signed-distance-field collision shapes with a friction coefficient of 8 (static) and 7 (dynamic). We choose these friction values following manipulation simulation benchmarks such as RoboDojo [5] and RoboLab [48], so that objects can be reliably grasped in simulation.

Closed-loop rollout. Physics is stepped at 240 Hz, and control runs at 30 Hz. Each action chunk is executed for 50 control steps (1.67 s) before the next policy query; the episode is therefore closed loop, unlike the open-loop trajectory replay in Appendix C.5 \parOpen-loop trajectory replay protocol. An episode ends after 360 s, once both arms have been stationary for 10 s (fingertips and gripper joints moving less than 5 mm), or once no object has moved more than 5 mm for 60 s, counted from the first object motion. The same settings are used for the SceneRig and the SimFoundry rows.

Scoring. Simulated success is a task-specific geometric predicate on the final object centroids relative to the container at its final position. Plates and bowls use a circle fitted to the outer rim, cups and mugs a circle fitted to the wall (which excludes a mug’s handle), and bins the axis-aligned box of the bin mesh. Required objects are defined by the real scene: the fruit tasks require every fruit, mustard in bin requires the mustard bottle, and everything into the bin requires every object that did not start inside the bin. A required object missing from the reconstruction counts as a failure, and for everything into the bin, hallucinated objects must also be placed in the bin. A human scorer verifies the verdicts generated by the script. Real success is the operator’s verdict.

Metric aggregation. For each policy, agreement and Cohen’s κ\kappa use its 50 episodes, and Pearson’s rr correlates its five real and simulated task success rates. Combined agreement pools all 100 episodes. The pooled correlation is computed directly from all ten policy–task success-rate pairs. MMRV [21] averages, over policy–task pairs, the largest real success-rate gap to any pair whose simulated order contradicts the real order; lower is better. Confidence intervals come from 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples of episodes within each policy–task cell, and McNemar’s exact test compares the two methods’ per-episode agreement with the real verdicts. With five tasks per policy, the rate-level metrics (rr, MMRV, and rate error) are reported without intervals.

MMRV. We follow SIMPLER’s published formula [21], using strict << comparisons. For KK paired real and simulated success rates rir_{i} and sis_{i},

Vi​j=|ri−rj|[(si<sj)≠(ri<rj)],MMRV=1K∑i=1Kmax1≤j≤KVi​j.V_{ij}=|r_{i}-r_{j}|\,\mathbf{1\par}\!\left[\par(s_{i}<s_{j})\neq(r_{i}<r_{j})\right]\par,\qquad\mathrm{MMRV\par}=\frac{1\par}{K\par}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\max_{1\leq j\leq K}V_{ij}.

Across the ten pooled policy–task pairs, MMRV is 0.04 for SceneRig and 0.11 for SimFoundry (Table C.4 \parReal-to-sim policy evaluation protocol); lower is better.

SimFoundry inference. For the SimFoundry rows, the reconstructed objects are replaced by SimFoundry’s meshes, textures, poses, and masses, and registered into the station frame through the shared head camera. Since SimFoundry does not reconstruct table mesh, we borrow it from our method and paint the table with SimFoundry’s inpainted table image.

Agreement across policies. For LingBot-VLA 2.0, SceneRig achieves 66%

episode agreement (κ=0.25\kappa=0.25) versus 60%

(κ=0.09\kappa=0.09) for SimFoundry, with task-level correlations of r=0.93r=0.93 and r=0.88r=0.88, respectively. Both underestimate real-world success: SceneRig succeeds on 13/50 episodes and SimFoundry on 10/50, versus 20/50 on the real robot. The agreement advantage varies by task; SimFoundry agrees more often on fruits-to-bowl and marker-to-cup. Across both policies, SceneRig matches 69/100 real outcomes, versus 54/100 for SimFoundry. Figure combines their ten policy–task success-rate pairs, yielding pooled correlations of 0.920.92 and 0.840.84. These correlations capture variation across both policies and tasks; the tables report each policy separately.

Statistical analysis. Table C.4 \parReal-to-sim policy evaluation protocol adds uncertainty estimates and paired tests. Pooled over both policies, SceneRig’s agreement advantage is significant (25 vs. 10 discordant episodes, McNemar p=0.017p=0.017), and its κ\kappa exceeds SimFoundry’s by 0.29 (95%

CI [0.08, 0.50]).

C.5 \parOpen-loop trajectory replay protocol

This section details the open-loop trajectory replay experiment in Section . Unlike the evaluation in Section , which queries the policy between action chunks, this experiment executes an entire command sequence recorded on the real robot without additional policy inference.

Episodes. We evaluate 25 successful teleoperated demonstrations recorded on a bimanual station of the same design, with arm-base and head-camera poses calibrated using a ChArUco board before recording. There are five demonstrations per task: everything into the bin, cup into the bowl, fruits from the plate into the bowl, marker into the cup, and mustard bottle into the bin. The demonstrations involve 1–6 evaluated objects each. We replay the recorded follower’s joint trajectory, logged at 30–60 Hz depending on the session, rather than the leader commands, so that the simulated arm follows the motion observed in the recording.

Scene construction and registration. Both methods receive the same armless head-camera image and metric depth input as in Appendix C.4 \parReal-to-sim policy evaluation protocol. For each episode, we import the reconstructed textured geometry and estimated physical properties into Isaac Sim. We align the reconstructed scene to the station frame using the calibrated head-camera pose. The simulated rig uses the measured robot-base poses and the camera’s measured intrinsics. Collision geometry is derived from the reconstructed object meshes, the tabletop is a static prism collider at the measured height, and the robot is initialized from the episode’s recorded joint configuration. For SimFoundry, we register its objects into the same rig frame through the head camera, as in the object-replacement protocol above, keep its estimated object masses, assign friction from our material table by object category, and replay the same command stream in the same calibrated robot setup. SimFoundry scenes are rendered with its inpainted table texture and SceneRig scenes with the reconstruction’s own tabletop.

Command replay. Physics is stepped at 240 Hz. After a 0.5 s settling period, we execute the time-stamped joint targets and gripper commands through the simulated controllers according to their recorded timing. The arm controller uses hardware-matched joint gains with full gravity feed-forward. After initialization, the robot follows the commands through simulated controllers, while objects move through the resulting contacts and dynamics. No policy queries, trajectory adaptation, or human intervention occur after replay begins.

Scoring. We score final object placements with the criteria in Appendix C.4 \parReal-to-sim policy evaluation protocol, including treating a missing required object as a failure, with automated verdicts reviewed against the real demonstrations by a human scorer. For everything-into-the-bin replay, objects already inside the bin are excluded from the placement count. We also exclude objects that the real demonstration leaves untouched. These exclusions apply to both methods; hallucinated objects are not exempt, so an episode fails if one remains outside the bin.

Replays succeed in 20 of 25 SceneRig scenes and 9 of 25 SimFoundry scenes (95%

Wilson intervals [61, 91]%

and [20, 55]%

). SceneRig succeeds on all nine demonstrations that SimFoundry replays successfully and on eleven more (exact McNemar p=0.001p=0.001). Across the SceneRig scenes, 39 of 45 evaluated objects reach their targets. Of the five unsuccessful replays, four leave one object unplaced and one leaves two. SimFoundry’s automatic object counts include extra instances and can omit missing or fused objects, so they do not provide a directly comparable object-level success fraction. We therefore compare the methods using the reviewed episode-level outcomes in Table .

Placement ablation. We repeat the same 25 demonstrations with the code-edits-only variant, which removes the bounded move tool while retaining direct scene-code edits and physical settling. Recorded commands, calibration, controllers, simulation settings, and scoring remain unchanged. This variant succeeds on 11/25 replays (44%

), compared with 20/25 (80%

) for full SceneRig (Table C.5 \parOpen-loop trajectory replay protocol). The full method improves success on four tasks and ties on mustard into the bin, supporting the value of the bounded move tool for placement fidelity in robot manipulation.

Appendix D \parAdditional Experiments

D.1 \parAblation Studies

Backbone comparison. Table D.1 \parAblation Studies evaluates SceneRig with different VLM backbones (main experiments use Claude Opus 5). GPT-6 Astra achieves the best results across all reported metrics, with the clearest gains in appearance. Object placement remains similar across backbones, suggesting that improved rendered similarity does not necessarily translate into comparable gains in 3D layout. Figure D.1 \parAblation Studies provides qualitative comparisons.

Physics-grounded object placement. Table D.1 \parAblation Studies compares raw SAM3D poses, the same poses after 5 s of PhysX settling, and SceneRig’s combined initialization and pose-refinement pipeline. All variants share segmentation, assets, camera, root surfaces, materials, and lighting. The SAM3D variants retain the shared gravity-aligned frame but bypass our metric pose initialization and refinement, gravity-based stability checks, and physical settling during reconstruction. The post-hoc variant applies its 5 s settling pass only after the raw-pose scene is assembled. Raw poses often violate support relations: 69%

of objects lie below their support surface (median 17 mm), and 15%

float above it. Only 2 of 80 scenes keep every object within 10 mm of its initial position after settling, and 46 of 80 within the 50 mm stability threshold. Post-hoc settling allows objects to reach resting configurations but can reduce segmentation overlap and 3D placement accuracy. SceneRig improves both alignment and placement while all 80 scenes pass the stability test. This comparison evaluates the combined placement pipeline, rather than isolating initialization and refinement individually. To assess the bounded move tool, the code-edits-only variant removes it from pose refinement while retaining the scene-code editing tool, which settles and renders each edit for agent review. It obtains lower instance overlap (ARI 0.858 vs. 0.878; FG-IoU 0.792 vs. 0.819) and object appearance (LPIPS∗ 0.178 vs. 0.170), while all 80 scenes remain stable. The replay ablation reveals a larger downstream gap: success falls from 80%

to 44%

without the bounded move tool (Table C.5 \parOpen-loop trajectory replay protocol). This suggests that aggregate reconstruction metrics can miss placement differences that matter for executing recorded robot motions.

D.2 \parAdditional Quantitative Results

Direct Codex harness with GPT-6 Astra. Codex [29] is OpenAI’s general-purpose coding-agent meta-harness: it gives the model shell and file tools but no task-specific structure. For the direct Codex baseline in Table D.1 \parAblation Studies, we attach each benchmark image to an isolated GPT-6 Astra session with ultra reasoning effort. We automate the runs through the non-interactive codex exec interface, using the prompt shown in Listing . The agent writes Blender Python, runs Blender headlessly, inspects rendered images, and iteratively refines the camera, geometry, materials, lighting, and composition. Each worker uses Blender 4.5.3 with Cycles on one assigned CUDA GPU, with a six-hour timeout per attempt and at most two attempts per image. Filesystem isolation prevents access to other scene workspaces and reconstruction results. The prompt prohibits external models, textures, images, and assets, and requires a final-render inspection followed by at least one refinement pass. It also requires one semantically labeled top-level Empty per independently movable object, with all of that object’s parts grouped beneath it, so that each object can be simulated as a single rigid body; environment geometry, cameras, and lights have separate roots. Required outputs are a procedural scene.py, a self-contained final.blend, its rendered final.png, and a report.json describing reconstruction decisions and known mismatches.

Reconstruction harnesses with shared VLM backbones. Table D.1 \parAblation Studies compares reconstruction harnesses with a shared VLM backbone. Both VIGA and the direct Codex harness receive an object-grouping instruction: all parts of each movable object share a parent Empty, allowing it to be simulated as a single rigid body. We run VIGA with medium reasoning effort and a 20-round budget for both backbones. With Claude Opus 5, SceneRig outperforms VIGA across appearance, instance structure, object placement, and physical stability. With GPT-6 Astra we compare against two baselines that share the backbone but not our harness. Neither VIGA nor the direct Codex harness has a physics stage, so we score their scenes after a 5 s PhysX settle with every object as a rigid body with its parts (primitives) being convex-hull colliders, letting floating and interpenetrating objects come to rest before the metrics are computed. Astra substantially improves VIGA’s appearance, and the Codex harness achieves the highest full-scene PSNR. SceneRig nevertheless achieves better instance segmentation, more accurate placement, and a higher stability pass rate: all 80 scenes pass, compared with 24 for VIGA and 16 for Codex, while OSPA@5 is 2.3 cm compared with 4.6 and 4.2 cm, respectively. These results indicate that improved image-space fidelity alone does not ensure accurate and stable object placement. SceneRig complements VLM reasoning with explicit scene structure, metric grounding, and physics-checked pose corrections; this comparison evaluates the complete harnesses rather than individual components. Figure D.1 \parAblation Studies illustrates the comparison.

Segmentation before and after 3D reconstruction. Table D.2 \parAdditional Quantitative Results scores each method’s own 2D instance segmentation of the input and the instance masks rendered from its final scene, against the simulator ground truth of the 44 grounded scenes. SceneRig achieves high input-mask agreement with the ground truth (ARI 0.981 and FG-IoU 0.970). In contrast, although REST3D and SceneConductor also segment well, their results degrade notably once objects are placed in 3D. The decline from input segmentation to rendered instance masks highlights errors introduced during lifting and reconstruction, including geometry, camera alignment, scale, and object placement.

D.3 \parAdditional Qualitative Results

Figure D.3 \parAdditional Qualitative Results extends the comparison to more scenes. Across these examples, SceneRig more closely preserves object arrangement, small items, and surrounding surfaces. The novel views reveal missing geometry and incorrect depth placement that can be less apparent from the input viewpoint, highlighting the importance of reconstructing individual objects and their spatial relationships.
